title: Dog
summary: Dogs have long been part of Indigenous life on Long Island as companions, household protectors, village animals, and beings with spiritual meaning. Early records show Native communities defending their dogs when colonial authorities tried to restrict or kill them.
content:
Dogs in Everyday Life

Dogs were part of Native life on Long Island before and after European contact. They lived close to homes and villages, helped watch over households, moved through camps and settlements, and appear in sources as animals people knew, kept, and defended. English writers sometimes described Native dogs as "young wolves trained up," but that wording reflects colonial judgment more than Native life. The stronger point is simpler: dogs belonged within Indigenous homes and communities. [1][2]

Why Dogs Became a Colonial Conflict

As English settlers brought more sheep, cattle, fences, and private-property rules onto Long Island, dogs became part of a larger fight over land and control. Settlers complained that Native dogs threatened livestock. Native people did not accept every order to kill or reduce their dogs. In 1680, Southampton settlers complained that Shinnecock people "utterly refuse" to kill dogs and continued to raise them. Records from 1718 show town officials still trying to force the issue. These were not just arguments about animals; they were arguments about who had authority over Native homes and daily life. [1][2]

Shinnecock and Montaukett Records

Montaukett records show the same pressure. In the eighteenth century, East Hampton officials restricted how many dogs Montaukett people could keep, and town trustees sent men to kill dogs in 1727 and 1742. A 1913 newspaper visitor to Shinnecock homes still noticed the "ever present watch dog" and wrote that every house visited had a dog. Read together, these records show both colonial interference and the long presence of dogs in Native household life. [5][6]

Home, Protection, and Spirit

Some sources connect dogs with hearths, homes, protection, and spiritual meaning. Dogs could be companions and guards, but they also carried deeper meaning in stories about family, women, children, death, and the journey beyond this life. The exact meaning was not the same in every place or moment, so the history does not turn dogs into one single custom. It keeps the focus on what can be responsibly said: dogs mattered in practical, emotional, and spiritual ways. [3][4]

References

  1. Peter Whiteley, Shinnecock Loss of Lands in New York (2006), citing James Truslow Adams, History of the Town of Southampton (1918), on colonial complaints about Native dogs and the 1680/1718 Southampton records.
  2. Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), discussion of Shinnecock dog conflicts and the importance of dogs in eastern Long Island Native cultures.
  3. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700 (1997), pp. 124-125, on dogs in Long Island Algonquian life and ceremonial interpretation.
  4. Gaynell Stone, ed., Long Island Native Americans: Selected Readings, discussion of Anne-Marie Cantwell's interpretation of dogs as beings between forest and camp.
  5. John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (2001), pp. 57-58, on Montaukett dog restrictions and 1727/1742 raids.
  6. "The Shinnecock Indians," The Brooklyn Daily Eagle, November 16, 1913, describing the presence of watchdogs at Shinnecock homes.
why_this_matters: Dogs are part of Indigenous Long Island history through everyday life: homes, safety, companionship, spirit, and colonial interference. Colonial records about dogs often say as much about English control over Native households, movement, and authority as they do about animals themselves. Native families continued to keep dogs as part of home, protection, companionship, and community memory.
